source.title: Assessment of the Mechanics of the Shoe-Turf Release Phenomenon Over a Range of Normal Loads

paper.citation: Koerber B., Gepner B., Jayathirtha M., Caldwell J., O’Cain C., Spratley E.M., et al. Assessment of the Mechanics of the Shoe-Turf Release Phenomenon Over a Range of Normal Loads. Source publication. 2026. doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-8904480/v1.
paper.abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Can a robotic compress-then-shear method repeatably identify cleat release, and is release shear force linearly related to normal force for one cleat-surrogate/artificial-turf pairing? Participants: No human participants; 24 mechanical tests. Sport and level: Test loads and cleat geometry were selected for relevance to elite American football. Design: Controlled laboratory method-development study. Exposure or intervention: Four normal-force preloads (0.7, 1.4, 2.1, 2.8 kN), posterior and lateral shear, three repeats per condition.
paper.tldr: Displacement magnitudes varied by <6%, temporal variability was within 30 ms, and CORA scores were ≥.97 across the 10.0–10.5-second shear interval. For the nominal 2,800-N condition (mean preload 2,573 N), posterior peak shear force was 4.45 kN, within one SD of prior BEAST testing (4.5±0.3 kN). The method is promising for controlled comparison of surface/cleat configurations across normal loads, but the reported regressions are engineering characteristics of one experimental pairing.
paper.methods: Design: Controlled laboratory method-development study. Exposure or intervention: Four normal-force preloads (0.7, 1.4, 2.1, 2.8 kN), posterior and lateral shear, three repeats per condition. Comparator: Direction and preload conditions within one turf/cleat pairing. Measurements and outcomes: Six-degree-of-freedom robot and load cell, synchronized 1,000-fps video, shear/normal force at observed release, and displacement repeatability. Analysis: Linear regression of release shear force on normal force and CORA comparison of repeated displacement histories.
paper.findings: Displacement magnitudes varied by <6%, temporal variability was within 30 ms, and CORA scores were ≥.97 across the 10.0–10.5-second shear interval. For the nominal 2,800-N condition (mean preload 2,573 N), posterior peak shear force was 4.45 kN, within one SD of prior BEAST testing (4.5±0.3 kN). High-speed video showed peak shear force immediately before the trapped turf fibers released from beneath the cleat surrogate. Release shear force was strongly linear with normal force within the tested range for posterior (R²=.96) and lateral shear (R²=.97).
paper.limitations: This is a preprint and had not completed peer review at the time of this record. A rigid aluminum cleat form did not represent deformable real footwear. Test translation speed was 0.3 m/s, 4–5 times slower than BEAST testing and slower than elite-player foot-displacement rates. Results were specific to one cleat–turf pairing, force range, ramp-out path, and construction; turf response varied and other orientations/materials may differ. Additional causal limitation — interpretation: Mechanical release thresholds cannot be translated directly into player injury risk or surface-safety rankings without athlete-level validation.
paper.practicalImplications: The method is promising for controlled comparison of surface/cleat configurations across normal loads, but the reported regressions are engineering characteristics of one experimental pairing. Facilities or performance staff should not treat these values as injury thresholds; applied decisions require standardized higher-rate testing across representative shoes, surfaces, environments, and player tasks.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete development, the method is promising for controlled comparison of surface/cleat configurations across normal loads, but the reported regressions are engineering characteristics of one experimental pairing. Facilities or performance staff should not treat these values as injury thresholds; applied decisions require standardized higher-rate testing across representative shoes, surfaces, environments, and player tasks. Apply the finding within the population and setting described in the source rather than treating it as a universal threshold.
paper.rtp: For rehabilitation and return-to-sport decisions, the method is promising for controlled comparison of surface/cleat configurations across normal loads, but the reported regressions are engineering characteristics of one experimental pairing. Facilities or performance staff should not treat these values as injury thresholds; applied decisions require standardized higher-rate testing across representative shoes, surfaces, environments, and player tasks. Use the paper as one input to interdisciplinary judgment, not as a standalone clearance criterion or reinjury prediction rule.
